# Typhon Cath CRM

**A production CRM for a local medical device company** — replacing two Excel spreadsheets with a role-gated web application, built by four students, deployed to a live client host.

`PHP` · `MySQL` · `JavaScript / jQuery` · `Docker` · `GitHub Actions`

|  |  |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Tests** | 217 tests, 569 assertions — unit \+ integration against real MySQL |
| **Pipeline** | 4 CI jobs, deploy gated behind all of them |
| **Schema** | 15 tables, 22 migrations |
| **Access control** | 5 roles, 40 permissions, enforced on all 42 entry points |
| **Team** | 4 developers, none with prior PHP experience |

---

## Overview

My capstone was a CRM for a local medical device company. On the surface this sounds like a simple weekend, we weren't inventing anything new, and we weren't solving a new problem.

That was exactly the opportunity. Because the domain was well understood, we didn't spend the semester figuring out *what* to build, which left room to figure out how to build it properly. The goal became not just a CRM that works, but one that models the real system of work, optimizes for the business's actual needs, ships with developer tooling like CI/CD, and takes security and performance seriously.

## What this replaced

The client was running their customer and sales pipeline out of two Excel spreadsheets, which are still in the repo as the original source of record. Everything the system does maps back to something someone was doing by hand: accounts and contacts, quotes moving through pipeline stages, stock reserved against open deals. That's the real measure of the project — not that a CRM is a novel idea, but that this one replaced a specific manual process for a specific business.

## Tech stack

The front end is JavaScript and jQuery over server-rendered PHP, with jQuery DataTables doing the heavy lifting on every list view — server-side search, sort, and paging. JavaScript was what elevated this to a modern web application while still accommodating the business requirement of a PHP stack. The backend is PHP against a MySQL database, running on Bluehost in production and in an isolated Docker container for local development and testing.

## Learning the stack

None of the four of us had written PHP before, and two had never built a web application at all. Ten years ago that would have meant spending half the semester on PHP and web fundamentals. In 2026 it didn't. Being able to lean on AI for the mechanical parts of an unfamiliar language meant we could step back and spend our time on the decisions that actually mattered — schema design, transaction boundaries, and how the modules would fit together.

---

## Architecture

Every module follows the same three layers: a controller per page, a service holding business rules and transaction boundaries, and a repository that owns all SQL. There's no framework and no router — a URL maps directly to a PHP file.

That uniformity was the point. With four developers who had never written PHP, a predictable shape meant anyone could open an unfamiliar module and know where things lived, and we could work in parallel without stepping on each other.

Request → public/modules/\<module\>/page.php

            → Controller      one method per page or POST handler

              → Service       business rules, validation, transactions

                → Repository  all SQL, nothing else writes a query

## Testing

217 tests across two suites: unit tests that need nothing and run in milliseconds, and integration tests against a real MySQL 8 instance rebuilt from the schema on every run. I used a real database rather than mocks because most of this application's logic *is* SQL — foreign keys, constraints, full-text search.

I also wrote two static harnesses that read the source and assert every entry point is CSRF-protected and permission-gated. Unit tests structurally can't catch a brand-new page that forgets one; these do.

## Security

Authentication and authorization are hand-rolled rather than pulled from a framework, which meant understanding every piece of them.

- **CSRF tokens** on every state-changing request, enforced by a harness that walks all 42 entry points — 185 checks  
- **Role-based access control** — 5 roles and 40 permissions, with the gate running *before* dispatch on every route, verified by 111 automated checks  
- **Authentication** — bcrypt with `password_verify`, session ID regeneration on login, and stale hashes upgraded transparently  
- **Login throttling**, session cookie flags, and idle plus absolute session timeouts  
- **Hardened responses** — security headers, no raw exception text ever returned to the browser, and a document-root `.htaccess` that denies logs, `.env`, and `.sql` files

## CI/CD

Every push runs four jobs — lint, security-wiring checks, unit tests, and integration tests against a MySQL service container — and deployment is a fifth job gated behind all four, so nothing reaches the live site on a failing build.

The upload is `lftp` driven directly rather than a third-party GitHub Action. That's a deliberate choice: it means the only things that ever touch the FTP credentials are the runner and lftp itself.

## Deployment

The document root points at `public/`, so application code, database scripts, and configuration sit one level *above* the web root where no HTTP request can reach them. Server-owned files — credentials, uploads, logs — are explicitly excluded from the deploy, so a release never overwrites production state.

---

## Modules

The modules were discrete and well defined, which gave us a strong base to work from. Each corresponds to a view in the application, with a dashboard that pulls all of them into one role-checked place so every user sees exactly what they have access to.  
![][image1]

### RFQ — quote and pipeline tracking

**Required**

- RFQ creation and tracking, linked to customers  
- Pipeline stages: New → In Review → Quoted → Negotiation → Won / Lost  
- Quote tracking: amount, discount, validity period  
- Deal conversion — RFQ into a "Deal Won"  
- Cross-module linkage: RFQ → Customer, RFQ → Inventory

**Built beyond scope**

- Win Rate by Account analytics page  
- RFQ summary page with analytics tables  
- PDF export of a single RFQ  
- CSV export of the pipeline respecting the current filter and view  
- DataTables server-side search, sort, and paging  
- Typeahead lookup endpoints for accounts, contacts, and products  
- Multiple quotes per RFQ, each editable and deletable  
- Reservation editing with a Reserved / Released / Converted lifecycle  
- **Transactional stage change** — winning an RFQ converts all its reservations atomically

### Customer — accounts, contacts, interactions

**Required**

- Customer profile creation and maintenance, contact management, interaction history  
- Customer records: name/company, email, phone, address, industry, tags  
- Search by name, email, and tags  
- Interaction logging: calls, emails, notes, meeting history

**Built beyond scope**

- Account detail page with a recent-interactions panel  
- PDF export of an account  
- CSV export and DataTables server-side processing  
- Faceted filter dropdowns built from distinct column values  
- FULLTEXT search indexes rather than plain `LIKE`

### Inventory — catalog, stock, allocation

**Required**

- Product catalog: name, SKU, price, description  
- Stock tracking: available and reserved quantity  
- Inventory allocation — stock reserved against RFQs

**Built beyond scope**

- Append-only inventory movements ledger, plus a printable ledger report  
- Per-product low-stock threshold and flagging  
- Delete guard that explains *why* a product can't be removed instead of throwing a database error  
- Stock released or converted automatically on reservation status change  
- Heavily-reserved ratio reporting  
- CSV export and DataTables server-side processing

### Admin — users, roles, permissions

**Required**

- Full system access, user management, system configuration  
- Distinguish the three non-admin roles: Sales User, Marketing User, Inventory Manager

**Built beyond scope** — the SRS never specified an admin module, so effectively all of it

- Permission matrix editor — 40 permissions × roles, editable in the UI  
- Custom role creation and deletion beyond the four named roles  
- A fifth role, Super Admin, which bypasses the matrix as a break-glass account  
- Login throttling  
- App-wide CSRF protection enforced by a test that walks every entry point  
- CSV export and DataTables server-side processing for the user list

### Dashboard — the integration layer

**Required**

- Cross-module data sharing, unified dashboard, internal APIs for module communication  
- Dashboard showing customer count, active RFQs, campaign performance, inventory status  
- Cross-module linkage: RFQ → Customer, Campaign → Customer, RFQ → Inventory

**Built beyond scope**

- 19 cards where the brief named 4 metrics  
- Per-card permission gating — a card hides itself if the user can't see its data  
- A `DashboardCard` abstraction with 19 subclasses, so a new card is one file  
- RFQ value by stage, win rate by account, expiring quotes, recent RFQs, recent interactions  
- Campaign reach, status breakdown, drafts, overdue sends, recent sends, upcoming sends  
- Low stock, pending reservations, reserved units, top reserved, heavily reserved  
- One memoised campaign-stats query shared across four cards

---

## Team

We split the four modules by owner: Casey took Inventory, Max took Customer Management and PDF generation, and I took RFQ, Campaigns, Dashboard, and Admin. Because the modules were well-bounded, we could work independently and integrate through a shared schema rather than constantly coordinating.

## My role

I owned the RFQ pipeline, campaigns, the dashboard, and the admin and permissions system, plus most of the shared foundation — the database schema and indexing, the role-based access control, the CSRF layer, and the DataTables integration the other modules' list views were built on.

Because I was working across module boundaries, I also picked up the integration work: the test suite, the CI/CD pipeline, and the cross-cutting bugs that only surface where two modules meet — like an RFQ moving to Won needing to convert inventory reservations atomically.

It's the role I'd want again. Building the parts everyone else builds on is where I learned the most.
